newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire army reinforces strategic towns.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army reinforces strategic towns.

text.p: Zaire's army said on Friday it was reinforcing the sprawling nation's third city of Kisangani, headquarters for its operations in the civil war zone in the east and strategic towns to the north and south.
Earlier, a senior defence ministry official told Reuters Zaire's army had won a fierce battle with rebels on Wednesday for a key bridge near Lubutu on the main road to Kisangani.
"The situation is stationary. On all the main fronts, nothing has been reported. Things have not changed... The rebels hold their towns, we hold ours," he said later.
The official said that reinforcements were being sent to Kisangani from the capital Kinshasa and from Kisangani to the towns of Buta, to the north, and Kindu, to the south.
Buta is 280 km (170 miles) north of Kisangani while Kindu is 400 km (250 miles) south on the Zaire River.
"Kindu is a command post. It is of vital strategic importance," the official said of the air, rail and water transport hub with its large concentration of government troops.
The rebel threat near Buta, Kindu and Lubutu suggested a rebel plan to converge on Kisangani on at least three fronts.

The official said earlier that the army had won a battle for a bridge on the Osso River near Lubutu, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani. "These clashes killed more than 30 of the enemy who fled. They have pulled back a long way," he said.
Ethnic Tutsis launched the war in October, accusing Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them to neighbouring Rwanda, their ancestral home.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said after the fall of Isiro, 340 km (210 miles) northeast of Kisangani, that the Gbadolite jungle palace of President Mobutu Sese Seko was a target. Buta is 450 km (200 miles) east of the palace.
Kabila has given Mobutu, who had prostate surgery in Europe in August, until February 21 to begin talks on stepping down.

The official noted that the rebels, who hold major towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda, had not seized major centres in fighting triggered by the January 20 launch of the government much-heralded counter-offensive.

"What people do not seem to notice is that the rebels have mainly captured villages and towns where there were only a few gendarmes. They have not been able to take a town protected by infantrymen," he said.
The official said the army was reinforcing Kisangani with 2,000 battle-hardened paratroops from its 31st brigade, adding that the city had "become a fortress".
The official rejected rebel suggestions the army was using napalm: "It's untrue. Zaire has never used napalm in this war."
He acknowledged the army had used napalm to curb a revolt in the mineral-rich southern province of Shaba in the 1970s. "That brought condemnation from the international community," he said.
The official said the army had retaken Bafwasende in the northeast while rebels had taken Faradje in the northeast corner of the country near Sudan -- in both cases without a fight.

"There was no fighting in Bafwasende. When the army arrived there the rebels had already left. Likewise in Faradje, which is now in rebel hands, there was no fighting. The rebels moved in after the departure of our troops," he added.

Rebel activity around Lubutu has led to an exodus of Zaireans from nearby villages. Almost 200,000 trapped Rwandan Hutu refugee are clustered around the nearby village of Tingi Tingi but Kabila has ordered his forces to avoid the camp.
